title: Food tells the journey
hookLine: bagels, kubbeh, injera, shakshuka: the food follows the wanderings
carry: a map of everywhere we've been

lines: A FAMILY'S FOOD IS A MAP.
cards: Shakshuka. Say them out loud and you've crossed half a map. A ring of dough boiled and then baked.
Dumplings of semolina or rice with meat folded inside, simmered in a sour soup. A soft, spongy flatbread for tearing and scooping. Eggs cooked in a pan of tomatoes and peppers.
Each one sits on Jewish tables, and each came from somewhere else, with someone. A family's food is a map of everywhere they've lived.

teach.h: A WANDERING ARAMEAN WAS MY FATHER.
teach.b: The Torah already ties food to a journey. In Deuteronomy, a farmer brings the first fruits of the harvest in a basket and sets them before the altar.
He can't just hand them over; he has to tell a story, and it begins: "A wandering Aramean was my father." Down into Egypt, slavery, rescue, and finally this land and this fruit.

The basket is the end of the journey; the words are the road that led there. The Haggadah later reads the same Hebrew another way, as an Aramean who tried to destroy our father, meaning Laban chasing Jacob.
Two readings, one verse, both a story told over food.

teach.h: A MEAL EATEN TO REMEMBER A ROAD.
teach.b: The seder plate works the same way: matzah, the bread of affliction, and bitter herbs, a meal eaten to remember a road.

teach.h: NO FIRE ON SHABBAT, SO A SLOW POT.
teach.b: Then the laws of Shabbat shaped the stove itself. The Torah says: "Ye shall kindle no fire throughout your habitations upon the sabbath day."

So Jewish cooks in lands far apart found a way to a hot Saturday meal without lighting a fire: a pot started before sundown on Friday, left to cook slowly through the night. Ashkenazi families call theirs cholent.
Moroccan families make dafina. Sephardi families make hamin. Same law, different pots, depending on where the road went.

And the dishes in the hook trace those roads: bagels from the Jewish bakeries of Eastern Europe, kubbeh in the kitchens of Iraqi and Kurdish Jews, injera on the tables of Beta Israel in Ethiopia, shakshuka from North Africa.
When families moved, they carried recipes the way the farmer carried his story.

how: Jewish families keep dishes from the places their families have lived, cook slow Shabbat stews such as cholent, dafina and hamin that need no fire on Saturday, and tell the story of the Exodus over the foods of the Passover seder.

o: a braided bread baked fresh for the Sabbath table
a slow Shabbat stew started before sundown on Friday
a sweet fruit spread eaten at the Passover seder

games.q: you're a farmer at the altar with your first fruits in a basket. the harvest is in. what do you do now?
o: set the basket down and leave quietly.
tell the story of your family's wandering, down into Egypt and back.
announce how large this year's harvest was.
games.why: the farmer tells a story: a wandering Aramean was my father. the fruit is the end of the road, and the words are the road.

practice: Smell a dish from memory, something a parent, a grandparent or a friend made, or something from a culture you love, and hear the kitchen it came from.
Ask its story the way the farmer told his: where did it come from, who carried it here, what changed along the way? If you pray, you can give thanks in your own words for whoever carried it.

wordCard.voice: Cholent. The slow-cooked Shabbat stew Ashkenazi Jews started before sundown Friday, one of many names, dafina, hamin, for the same law of no fire on the Sabbath. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew, Deuteronomy 26:5: 'a wandering Aramean was my father,' read differently in the Haggadah.
